note: Economics round 3 (part B): macro-economics and the Nigerian economy - national income and its measurement, money and banking, inflation, deflation, unemployment, population, agriculture, industrialisation, trade, international trade, balance of payments, public finance, taxation, development and planning, with a national-income accounts table and a two-state population table as data passages.

passages.text:

passages.text:
The table gives population information for
two states in a year.

                    State A   State B

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, Country K's gross domestic product (GDP) by the expenditure method is
questions.A: ₦6,900 billion
questions.B: ₦6,500 billion
questions.C: ₦7,600 billion
questions.D: ₦6,100 billion

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, Country K's gross national product (GNP) is
questions.A: ₦6,500 billion
questions.B: ₦6,700 billion
questions.C: ₦6,300 billion
questions.D: ₦6,100 billion
questions.explanation: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad = 6,500 − 200 = ₦6,300 billion.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, Country K's net national product (NNP) is
questions.A: ₦6,700 billion
questions.B: ₦6,100 billion
questions.C: ₦6,300 billion
questions.D: ₦5,900 billion
questions.explanation: NNP = GNP − depreciation = 6,300 − 400 = ₦5,900 billion.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, Country K's balance of trade in the year was
questions.A: a surplus of ₦200 billion
questions.B: a deficit of ₦200 billion
questions.C: a deficit of ₦2,000 billion
questions.D: a surplus of ₦900 billion
questions.explanation: Balance of trade = exports − imports = 900 − 1,100 = −₦200 billion, a deficit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, Country K's per capita GDP is
questions.explanation: Per capita GDP = GDP ÷ population = ₦6,500 billion ÷ 50 million = ₦130,000.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, net investment in Country K was
questions.A: ₦400 billion
questions.B: ₦1,200 billion
questions.C: ₦1,600 billion
questions.D: ₦800 billion
questions.explanation: Net investment = gross investment − depreciation = 1,200 − 400 = ₦800 billion.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The negative net factor income from abroad in the table above means that
questions.A: Country K imported more goods than it exported
questions.B: foreigners earned more from Country K than its citizens earned abroad
questions.C: Country K's currency lost value during the year
questions.D: the government of Country K borrowed from abroad
questions.explanation: Net factor income = income earned abroad by residents − income earned at home by foreigners; a negative figure means the outflow of factor income was larger.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: If the price level in Country K rose by 30% between the base year and the year in the table, the real GDP of the year in base-year prices is
questions.A: ₦4,550 billion
questions.B: ₦8,450 billion
questions.C: ₦5,000 billion
questions.D: ₦6,500 billion
questions.explanation: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ price index × 100 = 6,500 ÷ 130 × 100 = ₦5,000 billion.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the population density of State A is
questions.A: 120 persons per km²
questions.B: 100 persons per km²
questions.C: 200 persons per km²
questions.D: 300 persons per km²
questions.explanation: Density = population ÷ area = 6,000,000 ÷ 20,000 km² = 300 persons per km².

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the population density of State B is
questions.A: 300 persons per km²
questions.B: 100 persons per km²
questions.C: 10 persons per km²
questions.D: 90 persons per km²

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the natural rate of population growth of State A is
questions.A: 1.5% per annum
questions.B: 4.5% per annum
questions.C: 3% per annum
questions.D: 6% per annum
questions.explanation: Natural growth = birth rate − death rate = 45 − 15 = 30 per 1,000 = 3%.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the natural increase in State B's population in the year was
questions.A: 90,000 people
questions.B: 60,000 people
questions.C: 10,000 people
questions.D: 30,000 people

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the state with the heavier dependency burden is
questions.A: State B, because 12% of its people are over 64
questions.B: State A, because over half of its people are children or elderly
questions.C: State B, because it has the larger land area
questions.D: State A, because it has the lower death rate
questions.explanation: Dependants (under 15 + over 64): State A 51%, State B 37%. A larger share of dependants means fewer workers support each dependant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Judging from the table above, the population pyramid of State A would have
questions.A: roughly equal width at every age
questions.B: a narrow base and a broad top
questions.C: a very broad base and a narrow top
questions.D: a broad top and a narrow middle
questions.explanation: High birth rates and 48% under 15 give a wide base; only 3% over 64 makes the top narrow: a typical developing-country pyramid.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Judging from the table above, which of the following policies is State A most likely to need urgently?
questions.A: policies to attract young immigrants
questions.B: more old people's homes and pension schemes
questions.C: incentives to raise the birth rate
questions.D: expansion of primary schools and child health services
questions.explanation: Nearly half the population of State A is below 15, so schools and child health services face the greatest pressure.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: National income is best defined as
questions.A: the total amount of money in circulation in a country
questions.B: the total money value of goods and services produced by a country in a year
questions.C: the revenue collected by the government in a year
questions.D: the total wages paid to workers in a country
questions.explanation: National income measures the flow of final output (or equivalently incomes) over a period, usually one year.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In the circular flow of income in a two-sector economy, households supply ______ to firms and receive ______ in return.
questions.A: taxes; subsidies
questions.B: goods and services; taxes
questions.C: factors of production; factor incomes
questions.D: savings; investment
questions.explanation: Households own the factors and sell their services to firms for wages, rent, interest and profit, which they spend on firms' output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Savings, taxes and imports are ______ from the circular flow of income, while investment, government spending and exports are ______.
questions.A: final goods; intermediate goods
questions.B: injections; leakages (withdrawals)
questions.C: transfer payments; subsidies
questions.D: leakages (withdrawals); injections
questions.explanation: Withdrawals take spending out of the flow; injections add spending that did not come from current domestic income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, the value of the simple multiplier is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A government increases its spending on roads by ₦200 billion in an economy where the marginal propensity to save is 0.25. The eventual increase in national income is
questions.A: ₦50 billion
questions.B: ₦250 billion
questions.C: ₦800 billion
questions.D: ₦200 billion
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1/MPS = 1/0.25 = 4; 4 × ₦200 billion = ₦800 billion.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A household with an income of ₦100,000 spends ₦85,000 and saves the rest. If its income rises to ₦120,000 and spending rises to ₦100,000, its marginal propensity to consume is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The equilibrium level of national income in a simple economy is reached when
questions.A: consumption equals total income
questions.B: planned saving equals planned investment
questions.C: exports equal imports
questions.D: government revenue equals its expenditure
questions.explanation: In the two-sector model, income is in equilibrium when withdrawals (savings) equal injections (investment).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Per capita income is a poor measure of the welfare of a country's citizens mainly because it
questions.A: excludes the output of the agricultural sector
questions.B: is always measured in a foreign currency
questions.C: says nothing about how income is distributed
questions.D: is calculated only once every ten years
questions.explanation: An average can hide extreme inequality: a few very rich people can raise per capita income while most remain poor.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A rise in a country's nominal national income accompanied by an equal percentage rise in prices means that real national income has
questions.A: fallen to zero
questions.B: risen by the same percentage
questions.C: doubled
questions.D: remained unchanged
questions.explanation: Real income adjusts for price changes; if prices and money income rise equally, the volume of goods is unchanged.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following would increase a country's national income?
questions.A: a rise in the prices of second-hand cars sold
questions.B: an increase in the output of its farms and factories
questions.C: an increase in pensions paid to retired workers
questions.D: a transfer of money from one bank to another
questions.explanation: Only new production of goods and services adds to national income; transfers and second-hand sales do not.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In an economy, the consumption function is C = 50 + 0.6Y (in ₦ billion) and investment is ₦70 billion. The equilibrium level of income is
questions.A: ₦200 billion
questions.B: ₦120 billion
questions.C: ₦300 billion
questions.D: ₦250 billion

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The average propensity to consume of a household whose income is ₦200,000 and whose consumption is ₦150,000 is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The three methods of measuring national income are the
questions.A: cash, credit and barter methods
questions.B: income, output and expenditure methods
questions.C: fiscal, monetary and physical methods
questions.D: primary, secondary and tertiary methods
questions.explanation: In principle all three give the same total because output produced equals income earned equals expenditure made.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When measuring national income by the output method, the value-added approach is used in order to
questions.A: exclude the services of the government
questions.B: include transfer payments
questions.C: avoid double counting
questions.D: measure only agricultural output
questions.explanation: Adding the full value of intermediate and final goods would count the same output more than once; value added counts each stage's contribution only.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A farmer sells cocoa beans to a processor for ₦200,000; the processor sells cocoa powder to a factory for ₦350,000; the factory sells chocolate to consumers for ₦600,000. The total value added is
questions.explanation: Value added = 200,000 + 150,000 + 250,000 = ₦600,000, the value of the final good.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Pensions and unemployment benefits paid by the government are excluded from national income because they are
questions.A: paid in cash rather than in goods
questions.B: transfer payments not made in return for current production
questions.C: too small to affect the total
questions.D: already counted as government expenditure
questions.explanation: Transfer payments redistribute existing income; no new output is produced in exchange for them.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The difference between GDP and GNP is
questions.A: indirect taxes less subsidies
questions.B: depreciation of capital
questions.C: net factor income from abroad
questions.D: the value of exports less imports
questions.explanation: GNP = GDP + income earned by residents abroad − income earned by foreigners at home.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: National income at factor cost is obtained from national income at market prices by
questions.A: adding net factor income from abroad
questions.B: adding indirect taxes and subtracting subsidies
questions.C: subtracting depreciation
questions.D: subtracting indirect taxes and adding subsidies
questions.explanation: Market prices include indirect taxes (which are not factor incomes) and exclude subsidies, so both adjustments are needed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country's GNP at market prices is ₦90 trillion, indirect taxes are ₦8 trillion, subsidies ₦2 trillion and depreciation ₦6 trillion. Its national income (NNP at factor cost) is
questions.A: ₦84 trillion
questions.B: ₦78 trillion
questions.C: ₦74 trillion
questions.D: ₦96 trillion
questions.explanation: NNP = 90 − 6 = 84; at factor cost = 84 − 8 + 2 = ₦78 trillion.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a problem in measuring national income in Nigeria?
questions.A: the fact that most Nigerians are paid in foreign currency
questions.B: the absence of any government statistical agency
questions.C: the large amount of unrecorded subsistence and informal-sector output
questions.D: the small size of the agricultural sector
questions.explanation: Output consumed by producers themselves and informal trade go largely unrecorded, so figures understate true output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A housewife's unpaid work at home is not counted in national income because
questions.A: it is a transfer payment
questions.B: it does not satisfy any human want
questions.C: it is counted as government expenditure
questions.D: it is not exchanged for money in the market
questions.explanation: National income counts market transactions; the same work done by a paid house-help would be counted.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The GDP deflator is used to
questions.A: measure the level of unemployment
questions.B: convert nominal GDP into real GDP
questions.C: calculate the balance of payments
questions.D: convert GDP into GNP
questions.explanation: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ deflator × 100; it removes the effect of price changes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's nominal GDP rose from ₦150 trillion to ₦180 trillion in a year in which prices rose by 20%. Real GDP
questions.A: rose by 40%
questions.B: rose by 20%
questions.C: was unchanged
questions.D: fell by 20%
questions.explanation: Real GDP in base prices = 180 ÷ 1.2 = ₦150 trillion, the same as before; the whole increase was inflation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In the income method, national income is obtained by adding
questions.A: exports, imports and net factor income
questions.B: consumption, investment and government spending
questions.C: the outputs of agriculture, industry and services
questions.D: wages, rent, interest and profit
questions.explanation: The income method sums the rewards of the factors of production, excluding transfer payments.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm sold goods worth ₦10 million but ₦1 million of these were made in the previous year and taken from stock. In this year's national income accounts,
questions.A: the full ₦10 million is counted as this year's output
questions.B: ₦9 million is counted, as the stock reduction is subtracted
questions.C: only the ₦1 million taken from stock is counted
questions.D: nothing is counted because the goods were sold to consumers
questions.explanation: Output is what was produced in the year; goods produced earlier were counted then, so the fall in stocks is deducted.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The most important function of money is to serve as a
questions.A: standard of deferred payment
questions.B: store of value
questions.C: medium of exchange
questions.D: unit of account
questions.explanation: Money's primary role is to overcome the difficulties of barter by being generally accepted in exchange.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Prices of goods in a supermarket are written in naira. Money here is serving as a
questions.A: standard of deferred payment
questions.B: medium of exchange
questions.C: store of value
questions.D: unit of account
questions.explanation: Money provides a common measure in which the values of different goods can be expressed and compared.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A contractor agrees to be paid ₦5 million when a building is completed in two years' time. Money here serves as a
questions.A: medium of exchange
questions.B: standard of deferred payment
questions.C: unit of account
questions.D: measure of value
questions.explanation: Money allows contracts involving future payments to be expressed and settled.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following qualities of money makes it possible to buy small items such as a sachet of water?
questions.A: portability
questions.B: durability
questions.C: divisibility
questions.D: homogeneity
questions.explanation: Money must be divisible into small units so that goods of low value can be bought.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A high rate of inflation weakens money's function as a
questions.A: means of payment
questions.B: medium of exchange
questions.C: unit of account
questions.D: store of value
questions.explanation: When prices rise fast, money loses purchasing power, so people are reluctant to hold it as a store of wealth.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Money supply M1 in Nigeria consists of
questions.A: only the notes and coins issued by the CBN
questions.B: currency in circulation and demand deposits
questions.C: savings and time deposits in banks
questions.D: treasury bills and government bonds
questions.explanation: M1 (narrow money) is currency outside banks plus current-account (demand) deposits.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The value of money is measured by
questions.A: the exchange rate with the US dollar
questions.B: the amount of gold backing it
questions.C: the quantity of goods and services it can buy
questions.D: the number of notes in circulation
questions.explanation: The value (purchasing power) of money varies inversely with the general price level.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a function of a commercial bank?
questions.A: controlling the money supply through the cash ratio
questions.B: issuing the country's currency notes and coins
questions.C: acting as banker to the federal government
questions.D: accepting deposits and granting loans to customers
questions.explanation: Commercial banks take deposits, lend, and provide payment services; the other functions belong to the central bank.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The Central Bank of Nigeria acts as lender of last resort. This means that it
questions.A: gives loans to individuals who cannot get bank loans
questions.B: lends to commercial banks that are in temporary difficulty
questions.C: borrows from the public when the government is short of funds
questions.D: lends only to foreign governments
questions.explanation: By lending to banks in difficulty, the central bank protects depositors and the stability of the banking system.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The CBN raises the monetary policy rate (MPR) from 18.75% to 22.75%. The most likely effect is that
questions.A: the money supply expands rapidly
questions.B: commercial banks lower their lending rates and borrowing rises
questions.C: commercial banks raise their lending rates and borrowing falls
questions.D: prices of goods rise faster
questions.explanation: The MPR is the rate at which the CBN lends to banks; raising it makes credit dearer and slows the growth of money supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The central bank sells government securities in the open market in order to
questions.A: reduce the rate of interest
questions.B: increase the money supply
questions.C: increase commercial bank lending
questions.D: reduce the money supply
questions.explanation: Buyers pay with bank deposits, reducing banks' reserves and their ability to lend; this is contractionary open-market operation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The cash (reserve) ratio is 20%. A commercial bank receives a new cash deposit of ₦500,000. The maximum total deposits the banking system can eventually create from it are
questions.explanation: Credit multiplier = 1/cash ratio = 1/0.2 = 5; 5 × ₦500,000 = ₦2,500,000.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The central bank instructs banks to lend more to agriculture and less to importers. This instrument of monetary policy is
questions.A: bank rate (monetary policy rate) policy
questions.B: open market operations in securities
questions.C: selective credit control (directives)
questions.D: moral suasion through persuasion
questions.explanation: Directives that specify how much banks may lend and to whom are selective (qualitative) credit controls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A bank's liquidity ratio requires it to hold a proportion of its deposits as
questions.A: buildings, vehicles and other fixed assets it owns
questions.B: long-term loans to manufacturing and mining firms
questions.C: shares and debentures in private limited companies
questions.D: cash and assets that can quickly be turned into cash
questions.explanation: Liquid assets (cash, treasury bills, call money) let the bank meet withdrawals; the ratio is also a monetary control tool.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following does NOT create money in the economy?
questions.A: a commercial bank granting an overdraft to a trader
questions.B: a customer withdrawing cash from his current account
questions.C: the central bank buying treasury bills from the public
questions.D: the central bank printing new currency notes
questions.explanation: Withdrawing cash only changes the form of money held; bank lending and central-bank purchases add to the money supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's introduction of new naira notes in 2022–23 and the withdrawal of old ones was mainly an exercise in
questions.A: converting the country to a barter economy
questions.B: devaluation of the naira
questions.C: currency redesign to control cash outside the banking system
questions.D: increasing the money supply
questions.explanation: The CBN said the redesign aimed to mop up excess cash held outside banks and curb counterfeiting.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A creditor refuses to accept a cheque but cannot lawfully refuse naira notes offered to settle the same debt. This is because naira notes are
questions.A: issued by the commercial banks
questions.B: made of gold or silver
questions.C: used only for international payments
questions.D: legal tender, which must by law be accepted
questions.explanation: Naira notes and coins are legal tender in Nigeria; a cheque is not, since it may be refused.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Bank deposits created by lending are called
questions.A: token money
questions.B: credit (or bank) money
questions.C: commodity money
questions.D: fiat currency
questions.explanation: When a bank grants a loan it credits the borrower's account, creating a deposit that can be spent.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Inflation is best defined as
questions.A: an increase in the value of money
questions.B: a rise in the price of one important good
questions.C: a persistent rise in the general price level
questions.D: a fall in the quantity of money in circulation
questions.explanation: Inflation refers to a sustained increase in the average level of prices, not a one-off rise in a single price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's consumer price index stood at 250 in January and 300 in December of the same year. The rate of inflation over the year was

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: During an oil boom, the government paid large salary arrears and spending rose sharply while output could not keep pace. The resulting inflation is
questions.A: cost-push inflation
questions.B: demand-pull inflation
questions.C: imported inflation
questions.D: structural deflation
questions.explanation: When total spending grows faster than the economy's capacity to produce, too much money chases too few goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A fall in the value of the naira raised the prices of imported machinery, drugs and wheat, pushing up prices generally. This is
questions.A: hyperinflation
questions.B: demand-pull inflation
questions.C: imported inflation
questions.D: creeping inflation
questions.explanation: When the domestic prices of imports rise because of foreign prices or exchange-rate changes, inflation is imported.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Inflation of 2–3% per year over a long period is described as
questions.A: stagflation
questions.B: hyperinflation
questions.C: galloping inflation
questions.D: creeping inflation
questions.explanation: Slow, steady rises in prices are creeping (mild) inflation; hyperinflation involves extremely rapid rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following groups is most likely to lose during inflation?
questions.A: borrowers who repay fixed sums
questions.B: pensioners on fixed incomes
questions.C: traders holding large stocks of goods
questions.D: owners of houses and land
questions.explanation: Fixed money incomes buy less as prices rise; debtors gain because they repay in money that is worth less.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A situation in which rising prices are accompanied by rising unemployment and stagnant output is
questions.A: deflation
questions.B: reflation
questions.C: stagflation
questions.D: hyperinflation
questions.explanation: Stagflation combines stagnation (low growth and high unemployment) with inflation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A fiscal measure to control inflation is
questions.A: increasing the monetary policy rate
questions.B: raising the cash reserve ratio of banks
questions.C: selling treasury bills to the public
questions.D: increasing taxes and reducing government spending
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy uses the budget (taxes and spending); the others are monetary policy instruments.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A monetary measure to control inflation is
questions.A: reducing government spending on roads
questions.B: raising the monetary policy rate
questions.C: increasing income tax rates
questions.D: reducing import duties
questions.explanation: A higher policy rate makes borrowing dearer, reducing credit and spending.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A trader borrowed ₦1 million at 15% interest in a year when inflation was 25%. The real rate of interest was approximately
questions.explanation: Real interest rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation rate = 15 − 25 = −10%; the lender lost purchasing power.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The instrument commonly used to measure the rate of inflation in Nigeria is the
questions.A: monetary policy rate
questions.B: exchange rate
questions.C: GDP growth rate
questions.D: consumer price index
questions.explanation: The National Bureau of Statistics computes the CPI from the prices of a basket of goods and services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Inflation discourages saving because
questions.A: banks refuse to accept deposits during inflation
questions.B: the purchasing power of money saved falls over time
questions.C: the government taxes all savings during inflation
questions.D: interest rates always rise above the inflation rate
questions.explanation: If prices rise faster than the interest earned, savers can buy less with their savings later than now.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The value of money and the general price level are
questions.A: unrelated
questions.B: directly related
questions.C: inversely related
questions.D: always equal
questions.explanation: When prices rise, each naira buys less, so the value of money falls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PT), if the money supply doubles while velocity and the volume of transactions stay constant, the price level will
questions.A: rise by 50%
questions.B: halve
questions.C: remain unchanged
questions.D: double
questions.explanation: With V and T fixed, P is proportional to M, so doubling M doubles P.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A rise in the price of a single good, such as tomatoes during the rainy season, is NOT inflation because
questions.A: tomatoes are not included in the price index
questions.B: inflation refers to a rise in the general level of prices
questions.C: the price of tomatoes never falls again
questions.D: inflation affects only imported goods
questions.explanation: A relative price change in one good is different from a sustained rise in the average of all prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Deflation is
questions.A: a slowing down of the rate of inflation
questions.B: a fall in the price of one good
questions.C: a persistent fall in the general price level
questions.D: a fall in the value of money
questions.explanation: Deflation is the opposite of inflation: the average level of prices falls and the value of money rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: During deflation, the group most likely to gain is
questions.A: producers of manufactured goods
questions.B: borrowers who owe fixed sums
questions.C: traders holding large stocks
questions.D: people on fixed incomes and creditors
questions.explanation: Falling prices raise the purchasing power of fixed money incomes and of the money repaid to lenders.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A likely effect of deflation on an economy is
questions.A: rapid expansion of investment
questions.B: rising unemployment as producers cut output
questions.C: an increase in the profits of firms
questions.D: a fall in the value of money
questions.explanation: Falling prices squeeze profits and lead firms to cut production and jobs; consumers also postpone purchases.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A slowing of the rate of inflation from 30% to 20% is called
questions.A: reflation
questions.B: deflation
questions.C: disinflation
questions.D: stagflation
questions.explanation: Disinflation is a fall in the rate of inflation; prices still rise, but more slowly. Deflation is an actual fall in prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A policy of increasing government spending and cutting interest rates to lift an economy out of deflation and depression is
questions.A: deregulation
questions.B: disinflation
questions.C: devaluation
questions.D: reflation
questions.explanation: Reflation deliberately expands demand to raise output, employment and prices after a slump.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A government wishing to correct deflation would most likely
questions.A: raise the cash reserve ratio of banks
questions.B: reduce taxes and increase its spending
questions.C: sell more treasury bills to the public
questions.D: increase income tax rates
questions.explanation: Expansionary fiscal policy injects spending into the economy to raise demand and prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Consumers often delay purchases during deflation because
questions.A: the government bans the purchase of luxuries
questions.B: goods become unavailable in the shops
questions.C: they expect prices to be lower in the future
questions.D: their money incomes rise faster than prices
questions.explanation: Expected falling prices make waiting rational, which further reduces demand and deepens the slump.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Deflation increases the real burden of debt because
questions.A: the nominal value of the debt is increased by law
questions.B: interest rates always rise during deflation
questions.C: banks demand immediate repayment of all loans
questions.D: the money repaid is worth more than the money borrowed
questions.explanation: With falling prices, the fixed sum a debtor repays commands more goods than the sum originally borrowed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following situations best describes deflation?
questions.A: the inflation rate falls from 15% to 12%
questions.B: the consumer price index falls from 120 to 115 over a year
questions.C: the price of petrol falls while all other prices rise
questions.D: the exchange rate of the naira falls against the dollar
questions.explanation: A falling price index means the general price level is falling, which is deflation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: During the Great Depression of the 1930s, falling prices, falling output and mass unemployment occurred together. This situation is best described as
questions.A: stagflation caused by rising oil prices
questions.B: demand-pull inflation with full employment
questions.C: deflation accompanied by depression
questions.D: hyperinflation caused by printing money
questions.explanation: Prices and output fell together in the 1930s, the classic combination of deflation and depression.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A shoemaker in Aba lost his job when cheap imported shoes flooded the market and the demand for locally made shoes collapsed. He is experiencing
questions.A: voluntary unemployment
questions.B: frictional unemployment
questions.C: seasonal unemployment
questions.D: structural unemployment
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment arises from a lasting change in the pattern of demand or technology in an industry.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Workers laid off during a general slump in economic activity are experiencing
questions.A: frictional unemployment
questions.B: cyclical unemployment
questions.C: seasonal unemployment
questions.D: residual unemployment
questions.explanation: Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment rises when total demand falls in a recession.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Rice farm labourers in Kebbi who have no work between the harvest and the next planting season are
questions.A: frictionally unemployed
questions.B: structurally unemployed
questions.C: seasonally unemployed
questions.D: cyclically unemployed
questions.explanation: Seasonal unemployment follows the calendar of activities in farming, construction and tourism.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A bank replaced its cashiers with ATMs and dismissed many of them. The cashiers are victims of
questions.A: voluntary unemployment
questions.B: seasonal unemployment
questions.C: frictional unemployment
questions.D: technological unemployment
questions.explanation: Technological unemployment results when machines take over jobs previously done by labour.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Ten men are employed on a family farm that could be worked just as well by six. The four extra workers illustrate
questions.A: frictional unemployment
questions.B: disguised (hidden) unemployment
questions.C: cyclical unemployment
questions.D: structural unemployment
questions.explanation: When workers add nothing to output (their marginal product is zero), they are disguisedly unemployed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A graduate engineer who works as a commercial motorcycle rider because he cannot find an engineering job is
questions.A: voluntarily unemployed
questions.B: frictionally unemployed
questions.C: underemployed
questions.D: fully employed
questions.explanation: Underemployment occurs when a worker's skills or hours are not fully used.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A labour force of 80 million contains 68 million employed people. The unemployment rate is
questions.explanation: Unemployed = 80 − 68 = 12 million; 12/80 × 100 = 15%.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a likely cause of the high rate of graduate unemployment in Nigeria?
questions.A: a shortage of people willing to attend university
questions.B: a mismatch between the skills taught and the skills employers need
questions.C: the very small number of universities in the country
questions.D: the high wages paid to all fresh graduates
questions.explanation: Many graduates lack the practical skills demanded by industry, while the economy creates too few formal jobs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A policy most likely to reduce structural unemployment is
questions.A: paying higher unemployment benefits
questions.B: increasing the money supply to raise total demand
questions.C: retraining workers in the skills demanded by growing industries
questions.D: reducing the school-leaving age
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment reflects a mismatch of skills, which retraining corrects; more demand alone does not.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The labour force of a country consists of
questions.A: children, full-time students and retired persons who receive pensions
questions.B: the whole population of the country including children and the aged
questions.C: all persons employed in the civil service and the public corporations
questions.D: all persons of working age who are working or actively seeking work
questions.explanation: Full-time students, the retired and those not seeking work are outside the labour force.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Rural-urban migration in Nigeria contributes to urban unemployment because
questions.A: rural areas have more jobs than the towns
questions.B: migrants arrive faster than the towns can create jobs
questions.C: migrants refuse to accept any paid employment
questions.D: urban wages fall below rural wages
questions.explanation: Young people move to cities in search of better-paid work, but formal urban jobs grow more slowly than the number of arrivals.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The natural rate of unemployment consists of
questions.A: voluntary unemployment only
questions.B: cyclical and seasonal unemployment
questions.C: frictional and structural unemployment
questions.D: disguised unemployment only
questions.explanation: Even at full employment some workers are between jobs or lack current skills; this is the natural rate.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An economic consequence of high unemployment is
questions.A: a fall in the crime rate
questions.B: a rise in the level of national income
questions.C: an increase in government tax revenue
questions.D: a loss of output that could have been produced
questions.explanation: Idle labour means the economy produces below its potential; tax revenue falls and social problems rise.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The Nigerian government's N-Power and similar schemes were mainly intended to
questions.A: reduce the number of universities in the country
questions.B: provide skills and temporary jobs for unemployed youths
questions.C: raise the retirement age of civil servants
questions.D: restrict rural-urban migration by law
questions.explanation: Such programmes engage unemployed graduates and youths in public service and training to improve employability.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The census is important to a government mainly because it
questions.A: determines the prices of goods in the market
questions.B: increases the population of the country
questions.C: provides data for planning services such as schools and hospitals
questions.D: replaces the need to collect taxes
questions.explanation: Accurate population data are needed to plan, allocate resources and delimit constituencies.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country's population is 220 million and its labour force is 88 million. The dependency ratio is
questions.A: 0.67 dependants per worker
questions.B: 0.4 dependants per worker
questions.C: 2.5 dependants per worker
questions.D: 1.5 dependants per worker
questions.explanation: Dependants = 220 − 88 = 132 million; 132 ÷ 88 = 1.5.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A high dependency ratio in a country implies that
questions.A: the country has an ageing population only
questions.B: each worker supports many non-working people
questions.C: the birth rate is lower than the death rate
questions.D: most of the population is in paid employment
questions.explanation: A large share of children and old people relative to workers places a heavy burden on the working population.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Optimum population is the population size that
questions.A: the government of the day decides is ideal for the country
questions.B: is the largest number of people the country can possibly feed
questions.C: gives the highest output per head with the available resources
questions.D: has the lowest death rate and the highest life expectancy
questions.explanation: Below the optimum, more people would raise per capita output; above it, per capita output falls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country is said to be over-populated when
questions.A: most of its people live in cities
questions.B: its population is larger than that of its neighbours
questions.C: its population exceeds 100 million
questions.D: an increase in population reduces output per head
questions.explanation: Over-population is relative to resources, not absolute numbers: extra people lower average output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following would lead to a fall in a country's birth rate?
questions.A: an improvement in child health services
questions.B: wider education of women and later marriage
questions.C: early marriage of girls
questions.D: a rise in the number of polygamous families
questions.explanation: Educated women tend to marry later and have fewer children.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The main reason for the rapid growth of Nigeria's population since independence has been
questions.A: a rise in both birth and death rates
questions.B: large-scale immigration from Europe
questions.C: a high birth rate combined with a falling death rate
questions.D: the return of Nigerians from abroad
questions.explanation: Improved health care cut death rates while birth rates stayed high, so natural increase was rapid.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's population is described as youthful because
questions.A: there are more old people than young people
questions.B: most of the people are between 40 and 60 years
questions.C: the death rate is higher than the birth rate
questions.D: a large proportion of the people are below 15 years of age
questions.explanation: A high birth rate produces a population in which children make up a large share.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Net migration is
questions.A: the total number of people who leave a country
questions.B: the difference between immigration and emigration
questions.C: the movement of people from villages to towns
questions.D: the number of foreigners living in a country
questions.explanation: Population change = births − deaths + immigrants − emigrants; net migration is the last two combined.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is an economic effect of a rapidly growing population in a developing country?
questions.A: a fall in the demand for food
questions.B: a fall in the size of the labour force
questions.C: pressure on schools, hospitals and housing
questions.D: a reduction in unemployment
questions.explanation: Fast growth means more people to feed, educate and house, straining limited resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The population of a town rose from 500,000 to 600,000 in five years. Its average annual (simple) growth rate was
questions.explanation: Total growth = 100,000/500,000 = 20% over five years, or 4% per year on a simple basis.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which region of Nigeria has the highest population density?
questions.A: the Sahel zone of the far north
questions.B: the south-east and Lagos area
questions.C: the middle belt
questions.D: the mangrove swamps of the Niger Delta
questions.explanation: Lagos, Anambra and Imo are among the most densely populated parts of the country.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Malthus predicted that population growth would outstrip food supply. His prediction has not come true in most countries mainly because of
questions.A: the ban on migration between countries
questions.B: the rise in the death rate from wars
questions.C: improvements in agricultural technology and birth control
questions.D: the fall in the world's total population
questions.explanation: Modern farming methods raised food output far faster than Malthus expected, and family sizes fell with development.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The working population of a country is
questions.A: the total population minus children
questions.B: everybody aged between 0 and 64 years
questions.C: all the people who are currently employed
questions.D: the people of working age who are willing and able to work
questions.explanation: The working population (labour force) includes both the employed and the unemployed who are seeking work.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A major reason why many Nigerian farmers still produce small quantities is
questions.A: the ban on the use of fertilisers in Nigeria
questions.B: the land tenure system, which fragments farmland into small plots
questions.C: the very high wages paid to farm workers
questions.D: the absence of any demand for food crops
questions.explanation: Communal and inheritance-based tenure splits land into small scattered plots that discourage mechanisation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Agriculture contributes to Nigeria's industrial development mainly by
questions.A: producing the machinery and spare parts used by manufacturing industries
questions.B: providing electricity and water for the factories in the industrial estates
questions.C: supplying raw materials such as cotton, cocoa and palm oil to factories
questions.D: fixing the prices at which manufactured goods are sold in the markets
questions.explanation: Agro-based industries (textiles, beverages, soap) depend on farm produce as inputs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The main purpose of the commodity marketing boards in Nigeria before 1986 was to
questions.A: train farmers in modern farming methods through extension officers
questions.B: import food from abroad and sell it cheaply to consumers in the cities
questions.C: lend money to farmers at low interest rates for buying farm inputs
questions.D: buy export crops from farmers at fixed prices and sell them abroad
questions.explanation: Boards were monopoly buyers of cocoa, groundnuts, cotton and palm produce; the surplus they kept became a source of government revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Before the oil boom of the 1970s, Nigeria's main source of foreign exchange was
questions.A: the export of refined petroleum products such as petrol and kerosene
questions.B: the export of agricultural produce such as cocoa, groundnuts and palm oil
questions.C: revenue from foreign tourists visiting the country's game reserves
questions.D: the export of manufactured goods such as textiles and cement
questions.explanation: Groundnut pyramids in Kano, cocoa in the west and palm produce in the east dominated exports until crude oil took over.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A major problem of agricultural marketing in Nigeria is
questions.A: the ban on selling farm produce in urban markets
questions.B: the excessive use of machines by farmers
questions.C: poor roads and storage, which cause large post-harvest losses
questions.D: the small number of consumers who eat farm produce
questions.explanation: Much perishable produce spoils before reaching the market because of bad roads and lack of storage.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Plantation agriculture differs from peasant farming in that plantations
questions.A: are found only in the northern savannah
questions.B: produce only food for the farmer's family
questions.C: use small plots and simple tools
questions.D: grow a single cash crop on a large scale with hired labour
questions.explanation: Plantations (rubber, oil palm, cocoa estates) are large, specialised and commercially organised.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Guaranteed minimum prices for farm produce are intended to
questions.A: reduce the quantity of food produced
questions.B: protect farmers' incomes from sharp price falls
questions.C: raise the cost of food to consumers permanently
questions.D: discourage farmers from growing cash crops
questions.explanation: A price floor assures farmers of a minimum return, encouraging them to keep producing.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of the shifting cultivation practised by peasant farmers?
questions.A: it exhausts the soil permanently in one season
questions.B: it requires expensive machinery
questions.C: it wastes land and cannot support a large population
questions.D: it produces only export crops
questions.explanation: Leaving land fallow for years means large areas are needed to feed few people; it becomes impossible as population grows.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The Anchor Borrowers' Programme of the Central Bank of Nigeria was designed to
questions.A: replace the ministry of agriculture
questions.B: buy all rice produced in Nigeria at a fixed price
questions.C: import fertiliser for sale to large plantations only
questions.D: provide credit and inputs to smallholder farmers linked to processors
questions.explanation: Farmers received loans in the form of inputs and sold their output to anchor firms who helped recover the loans.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Farm mechanisation is difficult in much of southern Nigeria because
questions.A: farmers in the region are not allowed by law to buy or hire tractors
questions.B: farm plots are small and scattered and the terrain is often forested
questions.C: the soil of the region is too fertile to need any form of machinery
questions.D: there is no demand for the food crops grown on the farms of the region
questions.explanation: Tractors need large, cleared, consolidated fields to be economical.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Agricultural prices fluctuate more than the prices of manufactured goods mainly because
questions.A: manufactured goods are never affected by demand changes
questions.B: farmers change their prices every day for no reason
questions.C: farm output depends on weather and supply cannot respond quickly to price
questions.D: the government fixes the prices of all farm produce
questions.explanation: Supply shocks from weather and pests, combined with inelastic demand and supply, produce large price swings.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Agriculture in Nigeria is still the largest employer of labour, yet its share of GDP is much smaller than its share of employment. This shows that
questions.A: most farm output is exported
questions.B: farmers earn more than factory workers
questions.C: agriculture uses more capital than industry
questions.D: productivity per worker in agriculture is low
questions.explanation: When a sector employs many workers but produces relatively little output, output per worker is low.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Agricultural extension services are provided to
questions.A: buy farmers' produce at harvest time at guaranteed prices
questions.B: teach farmers improved methods and spread new technology
questions.C: collect taxes and levies from farmers in the rural areas
questions.D: build feeder roads and bridges in the main farming areas
questions.explanation: Extension workers link research institutes to farmers by demonstrating better seeds, fertiliser use and practices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A strategy of encouraging local factories to make goods that were previously imported is
questions.A: nationalisation of foreign companies
questions.B: export promotion industrialisation
questions.C: import substitution industrialisation
questions.D: regional economic integration
questions.explanation: Import substitution protects and promotes home industries to replace imports such as textiles and beverages.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a common problem of industrialisation in Nigeria?
questions.A: the absence of any raw materials
questions.B: an excess of skilled manpower
questions.C: very low cost of borrowing
questions.D: inadequate and unreliable electricity supply
questions.explanation: Firms spend heavily on generators and diesel because grid power is unreliable, raising costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Many Nigerian factories depend on imported raw materials and machines. A large fall in the value of the naira will therefore
questions.A: reduce their costs of production
questions.B: raise their costs of production
questions.C: have no effect on their costs
questions.D: increase the supply of local raw materials at once
questions.explanation: Imported inputs cost more naira when the currency depreciates.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Industries such as cement and quarrying are usually located near their raw materials because
questions.A: workers prefer to live in rural areas
questions.B: the finished products are more expensive to store
questions.C: the raw materials are bulky and lose weight in processing
questions.D: the government forbids them to locate in cities
questions.explanation: Transporting heavy limestone is costlier than moving the lighter finished cement, so factories sit near quarries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Breweries and soft-drink bottling plants tend to locate near large cities because
questions.A: they need cool weather to operate
questions.B: cities have the cheapest land
questions.C: their raw materials are found only in cities
questions.D: their products are bulky and their main market is the city
questions.explanation: Market-oriented industries locate near consumers to reduce the cost of distributing bulky or perishable products.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A cottage industry is one in which
questions.A: large machines are used in a big factory
questions.B: production is carried out in the home with simple tools
questions.C: the state owns all the equipment
questions.D: goods are produced mainly for export
questions.explanation: Weaving, pottery and local soap-making done at home are examples.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Small-scale industries are important in Nigeria mainly because they
questions.A: require no raw materials
questions.B: produce all the country's exports
questions.C: create many jobs with relatively little capital
questions.D: never face competition from imports
questions.explanation: Labour-intensive small firms spread employment and use local materials and skills.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The Ajaokuta Steel Company was intended to
questions.A: process cocoa beans into chocolate and beverages for export to Europe
questions.B: refine crude oil into petrol, diesel and kerosene for the domestic market
questions.C: assemble cars and lorries for export to other West African countries
questions.D: provide the basic industry for producing iron and steel for other industries
questions.explanation: Iron and steel is a basic (heavy) industry whose output feeds engineering and construction industries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Industrial estates and free trade zones such as the Lekki Free Zone are set up to
questions.A: prevent foreign firms from operating anywhere within the country's borders
questions.B: attract manufacturers with infrastructure and tax incentives in one location
questions.C: relocate all the factories in the big cities to the rural areas of the country
questions.D: increase the customs duties charged on goods imported into the country
questions.explanation: Concentrating services and incentives in one place lowers the cost of setting up and running factories.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Industrialisation can help a country's balance of payments by
questions.A: reducing the output of the agricultural sector
questions.B: increasing the import of consumer goods
questions.C: reducing imports and increasing exports of manufactured goods
questions.D: raising the price of foreign currency
questions.explanation: Home production replaces imports and may generate exports, both of which improve the current account.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Industries producing goods for immediate use by consumers, such as bread and soap, are
questions.A: construction industries
questions.B: heavy (capital goods) industries
questions.C: extractive industries
questions.D: light (consumer goods) industries
questions.explanation: Light industries make consumer goods; heavy industries make machinery, steel and other capital goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The localisation of industries in Lagos has produced external economies such as
questions.A: cheaper land than in rural areas
questions.B: a pool of skilled labour and specialised suppliers
questions.C: the absence of traffic congestion
questions.D: lower wages than elsewhere in the country
questions.explanation: Concentration of firms creates shared services, trained labour and supporting industries that benefit every firm.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A wholesaler differs from a retailer in that the wholesaler
questions.A: manufactures the goods that he sells in his own factory or workshop
questions.B: sells goods in small quantities directly to the final consumers
questions.C: buys in bulk from producers and sells in smaller lots to retailers
questions.D: operates only in the rural markets that are held on fixed days
questions.explanation: The wholesaler is the link between producers and retailers, breaking bulk and holding stock.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A trader buys goods from a Nigerian factory and sells them to consumers in Kano. This is
questions.A: bilateral trade
questions.B: foreign trade
questions.C: entrepôt trade
questions.D: home (domestic) trade
questions.explanation: Trade within the borders of one country is home trade.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A Lagos company imports electronics from China and re-exports them to Benin Republic. This is
questions.A: home trade
questions.B: entrepôt trade
questions.C: barter trade
questions.D: bilateral aid
questions.explanation: Entrepôt trade is the re-export of imported goods, often with little or no processing.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The naira was exchanged at ₦1,500 to $1 in January and ₦1,650 to $1 in June. The naira
questions.A: was revalued by the CBN
questions.B: appreciated against the dollar
questions.C: depreciated against the dollar
questions.D: remained stable against the dollar
questions.explanation: More naira are needed to buy one dollar, so the naira lost value.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An exporter sells goods worth $50,000 when the exchange rate is ₦1,600 to $1. The naira value of the goods is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A depreciation of the naira is expected to
questions.A: make Nigerian exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home
questions.B: make Nigerian exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home
questions.C: reduce the naira prices of imported goods
questions.D: have no effect on the prices of imports
questions.explanation: A weaker naira means foreigners pay less of their currency for Nigerian goods, while Nigerians pay more naira for imports.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's official adoption of a market-determined exchange rate in 2023 meant that the naira's value would be set mainly by
questions.A: the World Bank
questions.B: the President by decree
questions.C: the demand for and supply of foreign exchange
questions.D: the prices fixed by the bureau de change association
questions.explanation: Under a floating (market) system, the exchange rate is determined by market forces rather than fixed by the central bank.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The main advantage of a fixed exchange rate system is that it
questions.A: guarantees a balance of payments surplus
questions.B: allows the currency to adjust automatically to shocks
questions.C: requires no foreign reserves
questions.D: gives certainty to traders and investors
questions.explanation: Stable rates reduce exchange-rate risk in international contracts, though large reserves are needed to defend them.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Documents used in foreign trade include a bill of lading, which is
questions.A: a demand for payment sent by the exporter to the foreign importer
questions.B: a receipt for goods shipped and evidence of the contract of carriage
questions.C: a licence issued by the government permitting goods to be imported
questions.D: a certificate showing the country in which the goods were produced
questions.explanation: The bill of lading is issued by the shipping company and gives title to the goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A trader's goods are held at the port until she pays import duty. The duty is collected by the
questions.A: Federal Inland Revenue Service
questions.B: Central Bank of Nigeria
questions.C: Nigeria Customs Service
questions.D: Nigerian Ports Authority
questions.explanation: Customs administers duties on goods entering and leaving the country.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Middlemen in the distribution chain are often accused of
questions.A: paying too much tax to the government
questions.B: producing goods of poor quality
questions.C: refusing to buy from farmers
questions.D: raising prices to consumers by taking large margins
questions.explanation: Each link in a long chain adds a margin, so consumers may pay far more than farmers receive.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme aims to
questions.A: impose higher tariffs on goods from West Africa
questions.B: remove tariffs on goods originating within member states
questions.C: stop the movement of workers between member states
questions.D: replace the naira with a foreign currency
questions.explanation: Free movement of qualifying goods within the community is meant to expand intra-regional trade.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Country A can produce both rice and cloth more cheaply than Country B, but its advantage is greatest in rice. According to the principle of comparative advantage, Country A should
questions.A: specialise in cloth and import rice
questions.B: produce both goods and trade nothing
questions.C: specialise in rice and import cloth from Country B
questions.D: stop trading with Country B
questions.explanation: Each country gains by specialising in the good in which its comparative (relative) advantage is greatest, even if one has an absolute advantage in both.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country has an absolute advantage in producing a good when it can
questions.A: import the good more cheaply than it can make it
questions.B: produce the good at a lower opportunity cost only
questions.C: sell the good at a higher price than other countries
questions.D: produce more of the good with the same resources than another country
questions.explanation: Absolute advantage refers to greater productivity; comparative advantage refers to lower opportunity cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's export price index rose from 100 to 130 while its import price index rose from 100 to 104. Its terms of trade are
questions.A: 80, a deterioration
questions.B: 125, an improvement
questions.C: 104, unchanged
questions.D: 26, a deterioration
questions.explanation: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 = 130/104 × 100 = 125; a rise means each unit of exports buys more imports.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A tax imposed on imported goods is
questions.A: a quota
questions.B: an excise duty
questions.C: a tariff (customs duty)
questions.D: a subsidy
questions.explanation: Tariffs raise the price of imports to protect home producers and raise revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A government limits the quantity of rice that may be imported each year. This restriction is
questions.A: a subsidy
questions.B: a tariff
questions.C: an embargo
questions.D: a quota
questions.explanation: A quota is a quantitative restriction on imports; an embargo bans them completely.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria banned the importation of certain items and closed its land borders in 2019 mainly to
questions.A: increase the volume of imports
questions.B: protect local producers and curb smuggling
questions.C: encourage the dumping of foreign goods
questions.D: reduce the prices of imported food
questions.explanation: The measures were intended to boost local rice and poultry production and stop smuggled goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Dumping in international trade means
questions.A: importing goods without paying customs duty
questions.B: throwing away goods that cannot be sold
questions.C: selling goods abroad at a price below their cost or home price
questions.D: exporting goods that have expired
questions.explanation: Exporters may dump goods to capture foreign markets, harming the importing country's producers.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is an argument AGAINST protectionism?
questions.A: it protects strategic industries such as defence
questions.B: it protects infant industries until they mature
questions.C: it prevents the dumping of cheap foreign goods
questions.D: consumers pay higher prices and have less choice
questions.explanation: Tariffs and quotas raise prices, reduce choice and invite retaliation; the others are arguments for protection.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A Kano trader who sells grain in Lagos faces fewer difficulties than one who sells grain in Niger Republic mainly because trade across the border
questions.A: is always carried out by governments rather than by private firms
questions.B: involves different currencies, languages, laws and trade barriers
questions.C: does not involve the physical transport of goods from place to place
questions.D: is never affected by changes in the prices of the goods traded
questions.explanation: Exchange rates, customs regulations and immobility of factors between countries distinguish it from home trade.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country whose exports consist mainly of crude oil is vulnerable because
questions.A: it cannot import any manufactured goods from other countries
questions.B: crude oil is never demanded by the industrialised countries
questions.C: a fall in the world oil price sharply reduces its export earnings
questions.D: its currency will always appreciate against other currencies
questions.explanation: Over-dependence on one export makes government revenue and foreign exchange earnings unstable.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Free trade areas, customs unions and common markets are all forms of
questions.A: import substitution
questions.B: protectionism
questions.C: central planning
questions.D: economic integration
questions.explanation: They remove barriers between member states to varying degrees.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is intended to
questions.A: replace all African currencies with one currency
questions.B: create a single market for goods and services across Africa
questions.C: restrict trade between African and non-African countries
questions.D: abolish the customs services of African countries
questions.explanation: AfCFTA aims to remove tariffs and barriers on most goods traded among African countries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The gains from international trade include
questions.A: the removal of the need for a national currency
questions.B: the elimination of all unemployment
questions.C: a wider variety of goods and lower prices for consumers
questions.D: the end of competition between firms
questions.explanation: Specialisation and exchange raise world output and give consumers access to goods not produced at home.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Country P gives up 2 tonnes of yam for each tonne of rice it produces, while Country Q gives up 5 tonnes of yam per tonne of rice. Country Q has a comparative advantage in
questions.A: neither good
questions.B: rice
questions.C: both goods
questions.D: yam
questions.explanation: Q's opportunity cost of rice (5 yam) is higher than P's (2 yam), so Q has the lower opportunity cost in yam and should specialise in it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The balance of payments is
questions.A: the difference between the value of visible exports and visible imports
questions.B: a record of all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world in a year
questions.C: the amount of money a country owes to foreign banks
questions.D: the government's annual budget statement
questions.explanation: It includes trade in goods and services, income flows, transfers and capital movements.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is recorded as an invisible export for Nigeria?
questions.A: cocoa beans shipped to the Netherlands
questions.B: crude oil sold to India
questions.C: money spent by foreign tourists visiting Nigeria
questions.D: cars imported from Japan
questions.explanation: Services sold to foreigners (tourism, shipping, insurance, banking) are invisible exports.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In a year, a country's visible exports were $40 billion, visible imports $55 billion, invisible exports $20 billion and invisible imports $12 billion. Its current account balance was
questions.A: a surplus of $8 billion
questions.B: a surplus of $7 billion
questions.C: a deficit of $15 billion
questions.D: a deficit of $7 billion
questions.explanation: Trade balance = 40 − 55 = −15; invisible balance = 20 − 12 = +8; current account = −15 + 8 = −$7 billion.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country whose visible exports exceed its visible imports has
questions.A: an unfavourable balance of trade
questions.B: a favourable balance of trade
questions.C: a balance of payments deficit
questions.D: a capital account deficit
questions.explanation: The balance of trade compares merchandise (visible) exports and imports only.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Remittances sent home by Nigerians working abroad are recorded in the balance of payments as
questions.A: capital outflows
questions.B: visible exports
questions.C: current transfers (a credit)
questions.D: invisible imports
questions.explanation: Diaspora remittances are unrequited transfers that bring foreign exchange into the country.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A foreign company builds a new factory in Ogun State. This transaction appears in Nigeria's balance of payments as
questions.A: a current transfer out of the country
questions.B: an invisible import in the current account
questions.C: a visible export
questions.D: an inflow in the capital and financial account
questions.explanation: Foreign direct investment is recorded as a capital (financial) account inflow.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following measures would help to correct a persistent balance of payments deficit?
questions.A: removing all restrictions on imports
questions.B: devaluing the currency to make exports cheaper and imports dearer
questions.C: raising the exchange rate of the currency
questions.D: increasing government spending on imported goods
questions.explanation: Devaluation, import restrictions and export promotion all work to reduce a deficit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country finances a balance of payments deficit by
questions.A: raising the wages and salaries of its own workers
questions.B: printing more of its own currency notes and coins
questions.C: drawing on its foreign reserves or borrowing from abroad
questions.D: reducing the volume of goods that it exports abroad
questions.explanation: A deficit means foreign-currency payments exceed receipts; the gap is covered from reserves or by loans.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's external reserves are held mainly to
questions.A: settle international payments and support the value of the naira
questions.B: pay the monthly salaries of federal and state civil servants
questions.C: finance the construction of local roads and rural markets
questions.D: lend money in naira to commercial banks that are short of cash
questions.explanation: Reserves in foreign currency allow the country to meet import bills and intervene in the foreign exchange market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Devaluation improves the balance of payments only if
questions.A: the demand for exports and imports is sufficiently elastic
questions.B: the country imports nothing
questions.C: the demand for imports is perfectly inelastic
questions.D: foreign prices rise at the same time
questions.explanation: If demand is inelastic, cheaper exports earn less and dearer imports are still bought, so the balance may worsen.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A large fall in the world price of crude oil affects Nigeria's balance of payments mainly by
questions.A: reducing export earnings and the current account balance
questions.B: increasing the volume of manufactured exports
questions.C: reducing the demand for foreign exchange
questions.D: increasing the country's foreign reserves
questions.explanation: Oil makes up the bulk of Nigeria's export receipts, so a price fall widens the current account deficit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In balance of payments accounting, the payment of interest on Nigeria's foreign debt is recorded as
questions.A: an invisible import (debit) in the current account
questions.B: a visible import (debit) in the trade account
questions.C: a capital inflow in the financial account
questions.D: an invisible export (credit) in the current account
questions.explanation: Interest paid to foreign lenders is an outflow of factor income, part of the invisible (services and income) account.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The capital account of the balance of payments records
questions.A: flows of loans and investments between a country and the rest of the world
questions.B: exports and imports of physical goods such as oil, cocoa and machinery
questions.C: payments made for services such as shipping, insurance and banking
questions.D: gifts, grants and remittances received from or sent to other countries
questions.explanation: Foreign direct investment, portfolio investment and external borrowing appear in the capital and financial account.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Public finance is concerned with
questions.A: the revenue and expenditure of the government
questions.B: the profits of public limited companies
questions.C: the savings of private households
questions.D: the lending activities of commercial banks
questions.explanation: It studies how governments raise money (taxes, borrowing) and spend it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A budget in which planned revenue exceeds planned expenditure is
questions.A: a surplus budget
questions.B: a deficit budget
questions.C: a balanced budget
questions.D: a supplementary budget
questions.explanation: A surplus budget withdraws more from the economy than it injects and can be used to fight inflation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A government facing a recession is most likely to adopt
questions.A: a deficit budget to stimulate demand
questions.B: a surplus budget to reduce spending
questions.C: a balanced budget
questions.D: higher taxes on consumers
questions.explanation: Spending more than it collects injects demand into a depressed economy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The main source of revenue for Nigeria's federal government in recent decades has been
questions.A: receipts from crude oil and gas
questions.B: company income tax receipts
questions.C: personal income tax receipts
questions.D: revenue from foreign tourists
questions.explanation: Oil receipts have provided the largest share of federally collected revenue, though non-oil revenue has grown.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Government spending on roads, power stations and schools is classified as
questions.A: capital expenditure
questions.B: recurrent expenditure
questions.C: transfer payments
questions.D: debt servicing
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure creates long-lasting assets; recurrent expenditure covers salaries and running costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Salaries of civil servants and the running costs of ministries are
questions.A: recurrent expenditure
questions.B: capital expenditure
questions.C: development expenditure
questions.D: transfer payments
questions.explanation: Recurrent expenditure is repeated every year to keep government services running.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The national debt is
questions.A: the total amount owed by the government to its creditors at home and abroad
questions.B: the money the government spent in the current year
questions.C: the total value of goods imported in a year
questions.D: the money owed by all citizens to banks
questions.explanation: It accumulates from past budget deficits financed by borrowing.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Debt servicing refers to
questions.A: the payment of interest and repayment of principal on loans
questions.B: the borrowing of new loans by the government
questions.C: the cancellation of a country's debts
questions.D: the collection of taxes to finance the budget
questions.explanation: A large share of Nigeria's revenue has gone to servicing its domestic and external debt.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's Federation Account is
questions.A: the pool into which federally collected revenue is paid before being shared
questions.B: the account into which each state government pays its own internal revenue
questions.C: the account kept by the central bank for the salaries of federal workers
questions.D: the loan account that the federal government keeps with the World Bank
questions.explanation: Revenue in the Federation Account is distributed to the federal, state and local governments by an agreed formula.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a reason why the government borrows?
questions.A: to finance capital projects when tax revenue is insufficient
questions.B: to reduce the total supply of money in circulation
questions.C: to lower the level of national income
questions.D: to discourage private firms from investing
